title: The Alliance of Hawazin • On the Road to Hunayn • Dawn in the Valley • They Returned at a Single Call • The Witness for the Salab • The Uncle and Nephew of Awtas • Beneath the Fortress of Ta’if

blocks.1: Makkah fell so fast that before any tribe of Arabia could make sense of anything, it was all over. Those who accepted it with closed mouths bowed their heads in silence. But the necks of the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes were stiff. To sit quietly on this happy day of the Muslims offended their self-respect. They gathered around Malik ibn ‘Awf al-Nasri. The decision was made: fight the Muslims. He set out with the soldiers, taking along their wealth, women and children too. The thinking was: the one who has left family and goods behind him, where will he flee to? They came and pitched camp at Awtas. There was an old man there, Duraid ibn al-Simmah. Once a famous warrior; now he could not see, but his mind was still sharp. He asked, where are we? The people said, at Awtas. He said, a good place, just right for horses; neither hard nor soft. But from where is there coming to my ears the cry of camels, the braying of donkeys, the bleating of sheep and the weeping of children? Malik said, I have placed behind every soldier his family and property, so that they fight to protect them. Duraid said, lamb! Does anyone stop the defeated from fleeing? If you win, soldiers with arrows and swords will be of use; if you lose, you will be disgraced along with women, children and property. Malik replied, by Allah, I will not do that. You have grown old, and your intellect too is blunt. Either Hawazin will obey me, or I will put this sword into my belly and bring it out through my back. Duraid fell silent. He only said,
blocks.3: Alas, if only I were young today! Then I would run off at a trot. I would lead the horses with long hair and of middling kind.{{1}}
blocks.4: The old man could not see, but he had sensed the outcome. To the commander who counts his own stubbornness greater than listening, who explains the old man’s reckoning to him? Stubbornness sometimes turns all one’s own wealth against oneself. We do the same. The advice that is disliked we throw away as old; later we pay its price.
blocks.6: In the month of Shawwal, after nineteen days in Makkah, the Prophet {{1}} set out toward Hunayn. With him the ten thousand of Madinah, and a large band of the new Muslims of Makkah. He left ‘Attab ibn Usayd in charge of Makkah. He borrowed a hundred coats of mail from Safwan ibn Umayyah. A rider rushed in and brought news: I have seen from the top of such-and-such mountain, Hawazin, with their wealth, camels and goats, the whole tribe, have gathered at Hunayn. The Prophet {{2}} smiled and said, in sha’ Allah, tomorrow all this will be spoils for the Muslims.{{3}}
blocks.8: On the way there was a huge green jujube tree. Its name was Dhat Anwat. In the Jahili era the Arabs used to hang their weapons on that tree, slaughter animals beneath it, hold fairs. A few new people in the Muslim army said, O Messenger of Allah, as they have a Dhat Anwat, make one for us too. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.10: This is exactly what the people of Musa said, ‘Make for us a god too, as they have gods.’ By the One in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those before you.{{1}}
blocks.11: People who had only just left shirk. The marks of the old pictures still in their eyes. This mistake they made out of mere ignorance; the Prophet {{1}} corrected it at once. Seeing big trees, big shrines, big names, in us too the same desire stirs: let us make something for ourselves too, holding which we will get blessing. So the struggle of tawhid is not only against idols, but against the old mould of idols. Seeing the vast gathering of the army, from some people’s mouths it slipped out, today we are so many; today we will not lose. The word reached the Prophet’s {{2}} ears. He was deeply hurt.{{3}}
blocks.12: At Badr Allah helped three hundred and thirteen. Today twelve thousand. The help has not changed; what has changed is the address of reliance. The strength that relies on its own numbers, knowledge, rank, money, before it Allah sends a small test, so that it may remember who is the owner of everything.
blocks.14: That night Hawazin reached first. Malik ibn ‘Awf placed archers, two or four at a time, behind every cleft and cave of the valley of Hunayn. The order was, as soon as the Muslim army is seen, shoot arrows all together; then everyone will pounce. In the dim light of dawn the Prophet {{1}} drew up the army and distributed the banners. The army descended into the narrow valley. It did not occur to anyone that there could be people behind every rock. Suddenly a rain of arrows from all sides. Then the enemy pounced.{{2}}
blocks.15: Scattered. No one had time to look at anyone. Some men of Makkah, who had not yet brought Islam, shouted, today their magic has been caught. But who was on the field? Someone later asked Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA), did you flee on the day of Hunayn? He said,
blocks.17: I bear witness, the Prophet {{1}} did not retreat. The people who had rushed ahead in haste were the ones scattered; Hawazin showered arrows on them. And Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith was holding the head of his white mule, and the Prophet {{2}} was saying, I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the descendant of ‘Abd al-Muttalib.{{3}}
blocks.19: A man on a white mule, facing the enemy. His cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith holding the mule’s head, his uncle ‘Abbas pulling the stirrup. Everyone is telling him to turn back, to stop; he goes forward, singing, I am the Prophet, no lie. One who is on the truth can, in the face of fear, say his identity in an even louder voice. Even if a single man stands in a crowd of fleeing people, there the honour of the whole caravan is kept alive. The Qur’an has told of that day in this way,
blocks.21: In fact Allah has helped you in many places, and (especially) on the day of Hunayn, when your large numbers had made you proud. But that large number was of no use to you, and the earth, despite its vastness, became narrow for you. Then you turned your backs and fled from the battlefield.{{1}}
blocks.22: They Returned at a Single Call
blocks.23: The Prophet {{1}} said to his uncle ‘Abbas, call. ‘Abbas (RA) was a man of a very loud voice. As loudly as he could, he called,
blocks.25: Hey, Ashab al-Samurah, where are you?{{1}}
blocks.28: By Allah, on hearing my call they came back the way a cow returns on hearing the call of her calf. They began to say, labbayk, labbayk!{{1}}
blocks.30: Some could not turn their camels. They took off their iron mail, threw it over their necks, shield and sword in hand, let the camel go, and themselves ran toward the call. As soon as a hundred gathered, fighting again. The call went to the Ansar: Ya ma‘shar al-Ansar! The call to the Ansar narrowed further and finally came to rest on one branch of the Khazraj. The Prophet {{1}}, rising up on the mule’s back, looked toward the fighting and said,
blocks.32: Now the battlefield has heated up.{{1}}
blocks.33: Then he took a few pebbles in his hand and threw them toward the faces of the disbelievers. He said, by the Lord of Muhammad, they are defeated. Within a little while the situation reversed. The enemy who that morning had scattered the Muslims were now fleeing. Seventy leaders of the enemy side were killed. Six thousand prisoners, herds of camels and goats, four thousand uqiyyah of silver came into the Muslims’ hands. The Qur’an has told of that moment in this way,
blocks.35: Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and the believers, and sent down troops which you did not see. And He punished those who had disbelieved. And this is the recompense of the disbelievers.{{1}}
blocks.36: Allah sent an army that could not be seen with the eye. The one who relies on his own strength, his test comes through strength itself. The one who returns at a single call, for him help comes down from the sky. For returning, no day is too late. When we make a mistake we think, there is no road back. Those who returned at ‘Abbas’s one call, all of them had been fleeing only a moment before.
blocks.38: After the battle the Prophet {{1}} sat and announced,
blocks.40: Whoever has killed someone, and has proof for it, his is the salab.{{1}}
blocks.41: Abu Qatadah (RA) had seen that day a polytheist pressing hard on a Muslim. He had gone around from behind and struck that polytheist on the neck with his sword. He embraced him so tightly that he smelled death. Then the man died, he was freed. Hearing the Prophet’s {{1}} announcement Abu Qatadah stood up and said, who will bear witness for me? Then he sat down. The Prophet {{2}} said it again. He stood up again. Three times. The third time one man stood up and said, O Messenger of Allah, he has spoken the truth. His salab is with me. Please satisfy him on my behalf. Then Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) said, by Allah, that will not be. Leaving out one of Allah’s lions, who fights for Allah and His Messenger, will you be given his salab? The Prophet {{3}} said, he has spoken rightly. He gave the salab to Abu Qatadah. Abu Qatadah sold that mail and bought a date orchard. His first wealth in Islam. Claim, proof, witness. Even amid the excitement of the day of Hunayn these three steps were not skipped. When someone wanted to get a member of his own household something in place of bravery, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq stopped it, and the Messenger {{4}} called him right. For one who sits in the place of distributing, his task is to remember who is the rightful one; not who is sitting in front.
blocks.42: The Uncle and Nephew of Awtas
blocks.43: The fugitives split in three directions: some to Ta’if, some to Nakhlah, some to Awtas. The Prophet {{1}} sent an army toward Awtas with Abu ‘Amir (RA) as commander. With him his nephew Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari. There old Duraid ibn al-Simmah was killed. But an arrow shot by a Jushami polytheist went and pierced Abu ‘Amir’s knee. Abu Musa rushed up and asked, uncle, who struck you? Abu ‘Amir pointed, that is the man who shot me with the arrow. Abu Musa ran after him. The man began to flee. Abu Musa shouted, are you not ashamed? Stop! The man stopped. Two sword blows each passed between the two. Abu Musa killed him. Returning he said, uncle, Allah has killed your companion. Abu ‘Amir said, pull this arrow out. As it came out, water spurted from there. Abu ‘Amir said, nephew, give my salam to the Prophet {{2}}, and say, let him seek forgiveness for me. Abu ‘Amir made Abu Musa commander before he went. A little later he died. Abu Musa came back and went to the Prophet {{3}}. The Prophet {{4}} was then lying on a bed woven of palm-fibre rope; the marks of the bed had sunk into his back and ribs. Abu Musa gave all the news, and Abu ‘Amir’s salam. The Prophet {{5}} asked for water and made wudu’. He raised both hands. Abu Musa says, I saw the whiteness of his armpits. He said,
blocks.45: O Allah, forgive ‘Ubayd Abu ‘Amir. O Allah, on the Day of Resurrection place him above many of Your creation.{{1}}
blocks.47: Abu Musa then said, O Messenger of Allah, for me too. The Prophet {{1}} said, O Allah, forgive the sins of ‘Abdullah ibn Qays, and on the Day of Resurrection admit him to a place of honour. The last words of a commander on the battlefield were, tell the Prophet {{2}} to seek forgiveness for me. At the edge of death no one spoke of wealth, house, children. Only a du‘a. And the one from whom that du‘a was asked, leaving his busyness aside, made wudu’, raised his hands. When we hear news of someone’s illness we say, please make du‘a. How many of us raise our hands right then?
blocks.49: The greater part of the fugitives had gone and entered the fortress of Ta’if, with the commander Malik ibn ‘Awf. Having collected the spoils, the Prophet {{1}} went on the road to Ta’if. Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA) went ahead with a thousand soldiers. On the way Malik had a fort at a place called Liyyah. That was razed to the ground. Then the camp near the fortress of Ta’if. From inside the fortress arrows and heated iron spikes began to come down. Twelve Muslims were martyred, many were wounded. The camp had to be moved far away, to where today’s Ta’if mosque stands. The Prophet {{2}} set up a catapult, an attempt was made to breach the fortress walls. An attempt to enter under a wooden cover and burn the wall was also made, but it failed against the heated iron blades. After this the Prophet {{3}} said to cut down the grape orchards, to put the enemy under pressure. The Companions began to cut. Thaqif then, invoking Allah and kinship, asked to stop cutting the trees. The Prophet {{4}}, looking to Allah and kinship, stopped the cutting. It was announced, whoever leaves the fortress and comes to us is free. Twenty-three came out; one of them came down the wall hanging from a pulley, so he was named Abu Bakrah. The Prophet {{5}} freed them all.{{6}}
blocks.50: Days dragged on. The fortress did not budge. The Prophet {{1}} consulted Nawfal ibn Mu‘awiyah. He said, they are like a fox hiding in a hole; if you press hard you can catch it, if you leave it will not harm you. The Prophet {{2}} firmed up the intention to return.{{3}}
blocks.51: The moment it was said to the Companions it felt heavy. Return without victory? The Prophet {{1}} did not give a counter-argument to any argument. He only said, very well, go to the fighting tomorrow morning. They went. The result was wounds, blood, wounded companions. In the evening the Prophet {{2}} said again,
blocks.53: We are, in sha’ Allah, returning tomorrow.{{1}}
blocks.54: Now their hearts were cooled. Gladly they accepted, began to prepare for the return. Seeing this scene the Prophet {{1}} smiled. On the way back he taught the Companions a du‘a,
blocks.56: Say, we are returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord.{{1}}
blocks.57: Someone said, O Messenger of Allah, make a curse upon Thaqif. He made du‘a, O Allah, guide Thaqif, bring them back.{{1}}
blocks.58: The nation that was shooting arrows from the top of the fortress, shedding the Muslims’ blood — for it, what came to his lips was not a curse, but a prayer of guidance. And Allah had heard that prayer. The next year Thaqif themselves sent a delegation to Madinah. That story is in Dars 24. When we are struck by someone we curse; at words flung from the top of a fortress we get angry. And he was struck with arrows. Struck, he prayed for guidance. There is another lesson too. The leader does not always impose his own decision. Where people want to learn by first stumbling, he sometimes lets them stumble; then the right decision comes with a cool head. For the one whose decision it is, the duty is not only to announce it; it is also to know when the door of the listener’s heart will open.

footnotes.0: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 677–678 (Ibn Ishaq’s narration; Fath al-Bari 8/27, 42). Duraid ibn al-Simmah, the aged war-expert of Banu Jusham, still a disbeliever then; Malik ibn ‘Awf al-Nasri, the commander of Hawazin. A free rendering of the poem. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.1: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 679 (borrowing a hundred iron coats of mail with equipment from Safwan ibn Umayyah; appointing ‘Attab ibn Usayd in charge in Makkah; sending Abu Hadrad al-Aslami as a spy to the enemy camp). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.2: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 679 (the horseman’s news; the Prophet’s {{1}} smile and ‘in sha’ Allah tomorrow this will be spoils for the Muslims’; the guard of Anas ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi; the incident of Dhat Anwat). The ten thousand of the Madinah army and two thousand new Makkan Muslims, twelve thousand in all (al-Rahiq); in note 19 of Tawdih al-Qur’an the number of Muslim soldiers is fourteen thousand, in Bukhari 4333 Anas (RA): ‘ten thousand and the tulaqa’’. No number is set in the dars, because the sources do not agree. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.3: Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 2180 (from Abu Waqid al-Laythi (RA)); al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih. Musnad Ahmad 21897 (Arna’ut: the chain is sahih, on the condition of the two Shaykhs); al-Albani (Jilbab al-Mar’ah 202): sahih. In one version of al-Tirmidhi the incident is said to be ‘on the road to Khaybar’; in Ahmad’s narration ‘on the road to Hunayn’, and al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (pp. 679–680) also says so; so here it is the road to Hunayn. ‘Dhat Anwat’ is a jujube tree. The verse is Surah al-A‘raf 7:138.
footnotes.4: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:25, p. 530, note 19 (reading the printed page): ‘The Muslims had always won against greater armies despite their own small numbers. This time, since their numbers too were vast, from some of their mouths it slipped out that today our numbers are very many. So today we cannot be defeated by anyone at all. That the Muslims would rely on their own numbers instead of Allah the Exalted, this did not please Allah the Exalted.’ Al-Rahiq, p. 680: the Prophet {{1}} was deeply hurt by this remark.
footnotes.5: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 680 (at night Malik ibn ‘Awf’s placing of soldiers in the valley of Hunayn; at dawn the Prophet’s {{1}} arranging the army, distributing banners; the sudden rain of arrows; the separation of the vanguard of Banu Sulaym; the remark of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (RA) and the words of Kaladah ibn Hanbal). In Bukhari 4315 Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA): ‘the hasty people went ahead, Hawazin showered them with arrows.’ Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari 4315 (from Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA); via Abu Ishaq). On the same subject Ahmad 18468 (Arna’ut: the chain is sahih), Ibn Hibban 4770 (Arna’ut: sahih). The rajaz: ‘ana al-nabiyyu la kadhib, ana ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib’. The statement is not a poem; it came out of the mouth as rhythm.
footnotes.7: Disagreement on the number: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum, p. 681 (by Ibn Ishaq’s view nine; by Imam al-Nawawi’s view twelve; Musnad Ahmad 1/453–454 and al-Hakim 2/117, Ibn Mas‘ud (RA): eighty Muhajirun and Ansar; Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 1689, Ibn ‘Umar (RA): there were not even a hundred with him). The chain of the narration of eighty in Ahmad 4336 Arna’ut called weak, Ahmad Shakir called sahih; so no fixed number has been set in the dars.
footnotes.8: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:25, p. 530 (matched word for word by reading the printed page); note 19: a summary of the incident of Hunayn, the number of Muslim soldiers, the gathering of Banu Hawazin under Malik ibn ‘Awf, the archers’ sudden attack and ‘Abbas (RA)’s call.
footnotes.9: Sahih Muslim 1775 (from ‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA), via Kathir ibn al-‘Abbas; sahih): ‘That day I and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith did not leave the Prophet’s {{1}} side; when the Muslims drew back the Prophet {{2}} urged his white mule toward the disbelievers; I was holding the mule’s rein and stopping it; the Prophet {{3}} said, ‘Abbas, call Ashab al-Samurah’; ‘Abbas (RA) was a man of a very loud voice. ‘Samurah’ is the acacia tree of the Pledge of al-Ridwan; Ashab al-Samurah means the Companions of that pledge.
footnotes.10: Sahih Muslim 1775. In Sahih al-Bukhari 4333, Anas (RA): when the Prophet {{1}} said ‘ya ma‘shar al-Ansar’ they said, ‘labbayka ya Rasul Allah wa sa‘dayk, nahnu bayna yadayk’. By number the call to the Ansar was later narrowed down to ‘Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj’ (Muslim 1775).
footnotes.11: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 682 (‘Abbas (RA)’s call ‘O people of the acacia!’; whoever’s camel would not turn on the return would take off his iron mail, throw it over his neck, leave the mount and run toward the call with shield and sword; the attack as soon as a hundred gathered; the call at one point confined to Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj; the Prophet {{1}} threw a handful of earth and said ‘shahat al-wujuh’). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.12: Sahih Muslim 1775: ‘hadha hina hamiya al-watis’; later the Prophet {{1}} took a few pebbles and threw them toward the faces of the disbelievers, saying, ‘inhazamu wa rabbi Muhammad’, that is, by the Lord of Muhammad, they are defeated. ‘Watis’ is an oven or hearth; a proverb for the war reaching its peak. From Anas (RA), Bukhari 4333: the Prophet {{2}} dismounted from his mount and said, ‘ana ‘abdullahi wa rasuluhu’.
footnotes.13: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:26, p. 531 (matched word for word by reading the printed page); note 20: ‘in the hearts of the Muslims who returned on hearing ‘Abbas (RA)’s call Allah created such relief that the terror from the enemy side vanished.’ Note 19: seventy leaders of Banu Hawazin killed, Malik ibn ‘Awf left his family and wealth and took refuge in the fortress of Ta’if; six thousand prisoners; vast livestock and four thousand uqiyyah of silver as spoils.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 3142 (from Abu Qatadah (RA); sahih), Sunan Abi Dawud 2717 (al-Albani: sahih); Sahih Muslim 1751 also has the same incident. ‘Salab’: the weapons, armour and clothes found on a slain enemy. ‘La halla-hi idhan’: by Allah, never; ‘usd Allah’: Allah’s lion. This ruling of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) was endorsed by the Prophet {{1}}. ‘Makhraf’: a date orchard; Abu Qatadah (RA) sold the mail and bought an orchard among Banu Salimah.
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 4323, 2884, 6383; Sahih Muslim 2498 (from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari (RA); sahih): the Prophet {{1}} asked for water and made wudu’, raised both hands (Abu Musa says, I saw the whiteness of his armpits), then this du‘a. When Abu Musa asked for du‘a for himself he said, ‘O Allah, forgive the sins of ‘Abdullah ibn Qays and on the Day of Resurrection admit him to a place of honour.’ Bukhari and Muslim, both agreed upon.
footnotes.16: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 683 (the fleeing enemy splitting in three directions: one group to Ta’if, one to Nakhlah, one to Awtas; Abu ‘Amir al-Ash‘ari (RA) was the commander of the army sent toward Awtas, he was martyred there; the horsemen pursuing toward Nakhlah caught Duraid ibn al-Simmah and had him killed by Rabi‘ah ibn Rufay‘ (RA)). In Bukhari 4323 Abu Musa (RA): ‘Duraid was killed’. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.17: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 683–687 (the Ghazwah of Ta’if is the last part of Hunayn itself; the vanguard of a thousand soldiers of Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA); the razing of Malik ibn ‘Awf’s fort at Liyyah; the use of the manjaniq and a wooden ‘tank’ (dabbabah) toward the fortress wall, several martyred by thrown heated iron spikes; the martyrdom of twelve Muslims; stopping when Thaqif, on the cutting of the grape orchards, invoked Allah and kinship; twenty-three coming out on the announcement ‘whoever comes out of the fortress is free’, Abu Bakrah (RA) came down hanging on a pulley, hence the name ‘Abu Bakrah’). Disagreement on the time of the siege: forty days in the narration of Imam Muslim from Anas (RA) (al-Rahiq mentions); in others’ view twenty, eighteen, fifteen days; Fath al-Bari 8/45. On the chain of Abu Bakrah (RA)’s narration (al-Bazzar 9/132, Majma‘ al-Zawa’id 6/193) there is an objection of weakness because of Abu al-Minhal al-Bakrawi. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence. ‘The mosque of Ta’if’: al-Rahiq, p. 685: where the Companions moved the camp and returned to, a mosque was built there later.
footnotes.18: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 686 (the counsel of Nawfal ibn Mu‘awiyah al-Dili: ‘they are like a fox hiding in a hole; if you press hard you can catch it, if you leave it will not harm you’). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.19: Sahih al-Bukhari 4325 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA); sahih); Sahih Ibn Hibban 4779 (Arna’ut: the chain is sahih, on the condition of the two Shaykhs). The full narration: ‘The Prophet {{1}} besieged Ta’if, did not get anything from them. He said, in sha’ Allah we are returning. That felt heavy to the Companions; they said, return without conquest? The Prophet {{2}} said, go to the fighting in the morning. They went, were wounded. Then he said, we are returning tomorrow in sha’ Allah. That pleased them; the Prophet {{3}} laughed (Sufyan: smiled).’ In al-Rahiq (p. 686) this is told as the announcement incident of ‘Umar (RA); in the Bukhari text who made the announcement is not given.
footnotes.20: The original text of this du‘a on returning: Sahih al-Bukhari 3084 (‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA): the Prophet {{1}}, returning from a journey, would say takbir three times and say, ‘a’ibuna in sha’ Allahu ta’ibuna ‘abiduna hamiduna li-rabbina sajidun; sadaqa Allahu wa‘dahu wa nasara ‘abdahu wa hazama al-ahzaba wahdahu’); Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3440 (al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih; al-Albani: sahih). Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum, p. 687: on returning from Ta’if he told the Companions to recite this du‘a (Sirah-based part).
footnotes.21: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 687 (when some asked the Prophet {{1}} to curse Thaqif he said, ‘O Allah, guide Thaqif, bring them back’); this narration is in Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3942 (al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih gharib), but al-Albani in Da‘if al-Tirmidhi 3942 and Difa‘ ‘an al-Hadith 34 called it weak; because of Abu al-Zubayr’s ‘an‘anah, weakness of the chain in ‘Hidayat al-Ruwat 5941’. The sense of the incident agrees with other sahih narrations (Sahih al-Bukhari 3231, the first journey to Ta’if; Dars 9 of this series of dars). In this dars it has come only as a scene.

quiz.q: Who was the commander of Hawazin at Hunayn?
Who rebuked Malik with ‘lamb!’ for his decision to bring family and property along at Awtas?
quiz.e: None can stop the defeated from fleeing, he said.

quiz.q: What was ‘Dhat Anwat’?
o: The acacia of the Pledge of al-Ridwan
The gate of the fortress of Ta’if

quiz.q: On setting out for Hunayn, whom did the Prophet ﷺ leave in charge of Makkah?
quiz.e: The mail was borrowed from Safwan.

quiz.q: How many coats of mail did the Prophet ﷺ borrow from Safwan ibn Umayyah?
In the incident of Dhat Anwat, to what did the Prophet ﷺ liken the new Muslims’ request?
o: The demand of the people of Musa

quiz.q: What is learned from the statement ‘today we are so many, today we will not lose’?
o: Help comes by reliance on Allah
It is improper to fight without a big army
Taking new Muslims along was a mistake
Learning about the enemy is unnecessary

quiz.q: A new Muslim friend says ‘let us make something for ourselves too, holding which we will get blessing’; which incident does this match?
In which incident is the result of excessive reliance on one’s own numbers, knowledge or money seen?
o: The rain of arrows at the dawn of Hunayn
The martyrdom of Abu ‘Amir at Awtas
